source: original questions written against the public CCDV-F blueprint (Exam Guide v1.0)

questions.stem: A team is building a feature that takes a customer email, classifies it into one of five fixed categories, routes it to a category-specific prompt, and returns a templated reply. They propose a fully autonomous agent with a general tool set. Which approach is most effective?
options: Build an autonomous agent with all five prompts exposed as tools so it can decide which reply path to take.
Build a workflow: classify with one call, route to the category-specific prompt, and return the templated reply.
Build an autonomous agent and add a router agent in front of it to pick the category before the main agent runs.
Build the autonomous agent but cap it at a maximum of ten iterations to bound the cost.
questions.why: — The path is fully known and fixed, so a workflow is predictable, cheap, and testable. Exposing the five prompts as tools hands the model a decision it never needed to make; a router agent in front is just the workflow's router with an extra agent wrapped around it; and an iteration cap bounds cost but leaves the unnecessary nondeterminism in place.

questions.stem: A long-running research agent must read dozens of pages and then write a report. Its context fills with raw page text and it begins to lose the original instructions. Which approach is most effective?
options: Switch to a larger-context model so it can hold all the raw page text at once.
Use an orchestrator that dispatches a research subagent per source; each subagent returns only the extracted facts, and the orchestrator writes the report from those.
Give the single agent a summarization tool and instruct it to summarize each page before reading the next.
Split into one subagent per page but give every subagent the full tool set.
questions.why: — Subagents isolate context: each research subagent absorbs raw page text and returns a distilled fact, so the orchestrator holds only what the report needs. A larger-context model just delays the overflow; self-summarization is nondeterministic and still grows one context; and one subagent per page with the full tool set multiplies cost and hands report authority to every worker.

questions.stem: A developer needs an agent that reads files, runs tests, and edits code in a repository, with a permission prompt before any write. They plan to write a custom while-loop over the Messages API that parses tool_use blocks and implements its own approval flow. Which approach is most effective?
options: Build the custom loop so the approval flow can be tuned exactly as needed.
Build the custom loop but reuse the SDK's tool schemas by copy-pasting them into the code.
Use the Claude Agent SDK: configure built-in tools and a permission mode so writes require approval, and keep only the logic unique to their task.
Skip tools entirely and ask the model to output the file edits as text for the developer to apply by hand.
questions.why: — The SDK already ships the loop, built-in file and test tools, and a permission system, so the team writes only task-specific logic. A custom loop reimplements all of it and inherits the maintenance; copying schemas still leaves dispatch and approvals hand-rolled; and abandoning tools for text output discards the agentic capability the task requires.

questions.stem: An agent with shell access must be prevented from running destructive commands like 'rm -rf' or pushing to a protected branch, no matter what a prompt or a retrieved document says. Which mechanism is most effective?
options: Register a PreToolUse hook that inspects the command and blocks destructive patterns and protected-branch pushes before they execute.
Add 'never run destructive commands or push to protected branches' to the system prompt.
Use a more capable model, which follows safety instructions more reliably.
Log every command the agent runs so violations can be reviewed afterward.
questions.why: — A PreToolUse hook is deterministic code that runs before the tool call, so the block holds regardless of what the model was told or ingested. A prompt line is only a request that injected content can override; a more capable model improves compliance but gives no guarantee; and logging is detective, not preventive.

questions.stem: A multi-step agent that processes support tickets runs 30 or more tool calls per ticket. Its per-ticket cost and latency keep rising, and late in each run it ignores formatting rules set at the start. Which change is most effective?
options: Increase max_tokens so the model has more room to think on each call.
Switch to a larger-context model and keep the full history for every ticket.
Compact the conversation as it grows — summarize completed steps, prune stale tool output, cache the stable prefix — and offload bulky sub-tasks to subagents.
Reduce the agent to a single tool call per ticket so the context never grows.
questions.why: — Rising cost and ignored early instructions are the classic symptoms of context bloat, so the fix is active context management. Raising max_tokens adds output room but no hygiene; a bigger window only lets the bloat grow larger; and collapsing to one tool call removes the multi-step capability the task requires.

questions.stem: A team is building a multi-agent system where each step must pass a validated, typed object to the next, a human must approve before the final step, and the run must be resumable after a pause. Which approach is most effective?
options: Use an abstraction framework that models the workflow as a stateful graph with checkpointing and human-in-the-loop support (for example LangGraph), with typed step outputs.
Hand-roll the orchestration on the raw Messages API so nothing is constrained by a framework.
Use a single agent with a large system prompt describing all the steps and let it decide the order.
Give every agent the full tool set and let them message each other freely until the task completes.
questions.why: — Explicit state, resumability, human-in-the-loop, and typed handoffs are exactly what a stateful graph framework provides. Hand-rolling reimplements checkpointing and approvals; a single mega-prompt enforces no ordering and cannot resume; and free-form agent messaging with full tool sets removes the guarantees the requirements demand.

questions.stem: A regulated team must run an agent that touches customer data and requires that the data never leave their own VPC, while keeping full control of secrets and network egress. Operational speed is secondary. Which deployment approach best fits?
options: Self-host the agent loop with the Claude Agent SDK on their own compute so secrets, network egress, and data stay in their VPC.
Use an Anthropic-hosted managed agent, which removes the infrastructure burden entirely.
Use the managed agent but add a system-prompt instruction to keep the data private.
Use the managed agent and log all traffic for audit purposes.
questions.why: — Data residency, secret handling, and network isolation are the constraints, and self-hosting the loop keeps all three under the team's control. A managed agent sends data through the vendor's environment; a prompt instruction is not a data-residency control; and logging is not a residency mechanism.

questions.stem: A fact-checking subagent is being added to a research orchestrator. A developer proposes giving it the same full tool set as the writing agent so it 'can do anything it needs.' Which approach is most effective?
options: Give the fact-checker the full tool set so it is never blocked.
Merge the fact-checker into the writing agent so no tool set is duplicated.
Give every subagent in the system the full tool set for consistency.
Give the fact-checker the least tooling it needs — read-only retrieval and search — and keep the writing agent's write tools out of its tool set.
questions.why: — Subagents exist for context isolation and focused tooling, so the fact-checker should carry only read-only tools. Full tool sets defeat that purpose and widen the blast radius; merging it into the writer removes the independent check; and giving every subagent every tool multiplies cost and risk.

questions.stem: An EU insurance company wants Claude to summarize claim documents for human adjusters. The documents contain EU personal data that must be processed in the EU, adjusters read summaries within minutes, and volume spikes to thousands per hour. Which approach best fits the requirement?
options: Use the Message Batches API because it is cheaper, and let adjusters wait up to 24 hours for the summaries.
Send every document to the direct Anthropic API from the company's US servers to minimize latency.
Use the smallest, fastest model available and drop the region requirement, since the data is only summarized.
Process Claude in an EU region through a vendor offering regional processing (for example Bedrock or Vertex AI in an EU region) and call the realtime Messages API with streaming for the adjusters.
questions.why: — The credited option is the only one that satisfies both hard constraints at once: EU processing for residency and the realtime Messages API for the minutes-scale latency. The Batch API violates the adjuster SLA; US processing violates a legal residency requirement; and dropping the region requirement trades a compliance obligation away for speed.

questions.stem: A team edits the system prompt in production to fix a formatting issue. Overall answer quality drops, but nobody can tell whether the prompt change or a coincidental model-alias update caused it. What is the most effective response?
options: Revert the prompt change and keep editing the prompt live in production until quality recovers.
Version the system prompt and the model ID in source control, roll back to the last known-good combination, and add an eval suite as a gate for future prompt and model changes.
Switch to a more capable model so the prompt change matters less.
Add instructions to the prompt telling Claude to preserve the previous formatting and quality.
questions.why: — Versioning plus rollback to a known-good combination restores a reproducible state and prevents recurrence with an eval gate. Live editing has no record and cannot isolate cause; a bigger model adds a second uncontrolled variable; and adding more instructions compounds the untracked change.

questions.stem: A developer reports that Claude 'forgot' everything from the previous turn and keeps asking for information already provided. Their code sends only the newest user message on each call. What is the most effective fix?
options: Enable a session parameter on the Messages API so the server retains prior turns between calls.
Raise max_tokens so Claude has more room to remember earlier messages.
Add 'remember everything the user said earlier' to the system prompt.
Keep conversation state on the client and send the full messages array — prior user and assistant turns plus the new message — on every request, since the Messages API is stateless.
questions.why: — Statelessness is the root cause, so the fix is to resend the prior turns in the messages array. There is no server-side session parameter; max_tokens caps output length, not memory; and a system instruction cannot restore content the API never received.

questions.stem: A media company must summarize 50,000 archived recordings to build a searchable index. Nothing is user-facing, the index is needed next week, and cost is the main constraint. Which approach best fits?
options: Fire all 50,000 requests through the realtime Messages API concurrently to finish as fast as possible.
Submit the work as Message Batches, poll for completion, and reassemble the results by custom_id when the batch finishes.
Trim max_tokens on each summary to cut cost, then run everything synchronously.
Switch to the smallest model for every recording, regardless of summary quality.
questions.why: — Batch fits latency-tolerant, high-volume, cost-sensitive work and reassembles unordered results by custom_id. Concurrent realtime calls ignore the cost constraint and invite rate limits; trimming max_tokens degrades output without fixing the cost structure; and a blind model downgrade sacrifices quality without capturing the batch discount.

questions.stem: Under load, a service that calls Claude starts returning HTTP 429 rate-limit errors. The current retry loop immediately resends every failed request in a tight loop, making the overload worse. What is the most effective fix?
options: Retry with exponential backoff plus jitter, cap the number of attempts, and make the retried operation idempotent so a duplicate call cannot double-act.
Increase the retry count so more requests eventually succeed.
Lower max_tokens so requests are smaller and less likely to be rate-limited.
Switch to a smaller model, which has higher rate limits.
questions.why: — Backoff with jitter, a bounded attempt count, and idempotency is the standard remedy for 429s. More retries without backoff worsen the storm; max_tokens changes output length, not request rate; and a smaller model does not remove the client-side retry loop.

questions.stem: A team prototypes a customer-facing feature in claude.ai and it works well. They move the same prompt text into their API-backed app, but the answers are worse and the model no longer uses a tool it used before. What is the most effective next step?
options: Paste the original prompt into the system field and raise max_tokens until the answers match the prototype.
Switch to the most capable model so the same prompt produces comparable quality.

Recognize that the interface changed the inputs: re-create the needed system prompt, tools, and examples explicitly in the API request, then eval the app rather than assuming the prompt text transfers.
Add 'use the tools available' to the prompt and re-test.
questions.why: — claude.ai supplies its own system prompt and tooling that the raw API does not, so the fix is to supply the missing inputs and eval the result. Raising max_tokens changes output length, not missing tools; a bigger model cannot use tools you never declared; and 'use the tools available' is meaningless when no tools were declared.

questions.stem: A production Claude feature's outputs change overnight with no code deploy. The code references the model by a moving alias (for example 'latest'), and prompts are edited in a shared document. What is the most effective fix?
options: Ask the vendor to stop updating the alias so outputs stay stable.
Add a system instruction telling Claude to keep its answers consistent over time.
Switch to the most capable model, which changes less often.
Pin the model to a specific dated snapshot and move prompt templates into version-controlled files, then roll out changes through review and an eval gate.
questions.why: — A moving alias and a shared doc are exactly the unpinned-model and unversioned-prompt failures; pinning plus version control restores reproducibility. You cannot make a vendor freeze an alias; a prompt cannot stabilize changed inputs; and model tier is unrelated to pinning.

questions.stem: A developer declares a get_order tool in the request and expects Claude to run the lookup. The response comes back with stop_reason 'tool_use' and no order data. What is the most effective fix?
options: Enable a server-side execution flag so the API runs the tool and returns its result.
Raise max_tokens so the tool call has room to return its data.
Add 'execute every tool you are given' to the system prompt.
Treat the tool_use block as a request: run get_order in their own code and send the result back as a tool_result block in the next user message.
questions.why: — The API only returns a tool_use block; your code executes the tool and returns a tool_result. There is no server-side execution flag; max_tokens does not run anything; and a prompt instruction cannot make the API execute code it was never asked to run.

questions.stem: An interactive assistant feels slow because users wait for the full answer before any text appears. The requirement is a sub-second time to first token. What is the most effective fix?
options: Lower max_tokens so the whole response is produced faster.
Switch to a smaller model and keep the non-streaming call.
Enable streaming (stream: true) so text renders from server-sent events as it is generated.
Poll the API repeatedly until the full answer is available.
questions.why: — Streaming returns server-sent events so the first tokens render immediately, which is what time-to-first-token measures. Lowering max_tokens does not start rendering sooner; a smaller model still returns one body; and polling adds latency and cost.

questions.stem: A coding assistant sends an identical 20,000-token system prompt and tool-definition block on every one of thousands of daily requests, with only the user's question changing. The team wants to lower cost without reducing answer quality. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Cache the user's question on each call, since that is the part that changes.
Mark the stable system-and-tools prefix with cache_control so repeated calls read it at a fraction of the input rate, keeping the changing user input outside the cached prefix.
Shorten the system prompt and tool definitions by deleting rules until the token count drops.
Disable caching and reduce max_tokens so every response is shorter.
questions.why: — The cost is a large unchanging prefix sent thousands of times, which is exactly what prompt caching is for. Caching the volatile question means every call writes a cache it never reuses; deleting rules trades quality for tokens; and disabling caching leaves the big prefix at full price.

questions.stem: A developer must send a scanned receipt image plus a question to Claude and get structured extraction back. Which approach is most effective?
options: Paste the image's file path as plain text in the prompt.
Base64-encode the image and append it to the system prompt string.
Ask Claude to fetch the image from the local filesystem.
Include the image as an image content block (base64 or URL) alongside the text in the messages array.
questions.why: — Vision accepts image content blocks (base64 or URL) alongside text in the messages array. A file path is just a string the model cannot see; appending encoded bytes to the system prompt is not the image channel; and the model cannot read the local filesystem on its own.

questions.stem: A complex math reasoning task produces shallow answers; latency is acceptable but accuracy matters most. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Raise the temperature so the model explores more reasoning paths.
Add 'think step by step' and lower max_tokens to keep the answer concise.
Switch to the cheapest model and ask the same question again.
Enable extended thinking with a token budget so the model reasons before answering.
questions.why: — Extended thinking spends tokens reasoning before answering, which is what a hard accuracy-bound task needs. Higher temperature adds variety, not rigor; 'think step by step' with a low output cap leaves no room to reason; and the cheapest model trades away the capability the task needs.

questions.stem: A web request handler calls Claude synchronously and blocks a worker thread for seconds under load, starving the pool. What is the most effective fix?
options: Make the model call asynchronous (await it) and run independent calls concurrently so handlers are not blocked.
Add more worker threads to the pool so the blocking is absorbed.
Increase the HTTP timeout so the blocking call is acceptable.
Reduce max_tokens so each model call returns faster.
questions.why: — Model calls are network I/O, so the handler must await them and run independent calls concurrently instead of blocking a worker. Adding threads masks the blocking; a longer timeout keeps the block; and reducing max_tokens does not unblock the handler.

questions.stem: A batch job that sends confirmation emails is retried after a partial failure, and some customers receive duplicate emails. What is the most effective fix?
options: Increase the retry count so the job eventually completes.
Key the send by an idempotency key (or custom_id) and make the downstream action idempotent so a retry cannot duplicate the side effect.
Disable retries entirely so no email is ever sent twice.
Add a prompt instruction telling the model not to send duplicate emails.
questions.why: — A retried send must be safe to repeat, so key it by an idempotency key and make the downstream action idempotent. More retries duplicate more; disabling retries abandons recoverable failures; and a prompt instruction cannot prevent a duplicate side effect.

questions.stem: A developer wants to restructure a large prompt-and-integration monolith before adding features. Which approach is most effective?
options: Rewrite the whole monolith in one branch and ship it when it compiles.
Refactor in small, test-backed steps — extract the model client, centralize prompt templates — with an eval suite proving behavior is unchanged.
Leave the structure as is and add features, since it currently works.
Move the prompts into a shared document to reduce coupling.
questions.why: — Small, test-backed refactors with an eval suite let a refactor prove behavior is unchanged. A big-bang rewrite risks the whole system at once; doing nothing accrues the coupling; and moving prompts to a shared document removes version control rather than improving structure.

questions.stem: A production Claude app must pin plugin and MCP dependencies so an unreviewed update cannot change behavior, and keep API keys out of committed configuration. What is the most effective approach?
options: Pin plugin and MCP versions and store credentials in a secret store or environment variables, keeping them out of committed settings files.
Put the keys in settings.json for convenience and rely on the repository staying private.
Allow plugins to auto-update so the app always has the latest fixes.
Embed the keys in the system prompt so the model can call the tool directly.
questions.why: — Pinning plugin and MCP versions and keeping credentials in a secret store is the only option that controls change and protects secrets. Committing keys relies on repo privacy that a clone or fork breaks; auto-updating plugins admits unreviewed change; and a prompt is an echoed channel, not a secret store.

questions.stem: A team wants the newest Claude beta feature and also needs requests to stay inside their AWS account and region. Which approach best fits?
options: Use the direct Anthropic API and assume the feature behaves identically on every path.
Use Bedrock in the region and assume every direct-API feature is available there.
Call Claude through Amazon Bedrock in the required region, and verify the beta feature is available on that vendor before depending on it.
Send each request to both paths and use whichever responds first.
questions.why: — Bedrock in the required region keeps requests inside the account and region, and verifying feature availability avoids depending on a capability that lags the direct API. Assuming identical features across paths is the parity trap; and sending to both adds cost and an uncontrolled data path.

questions.stem: A platform team must ensure every developer in the organization inherits a mandatory security instruction that individual projects cannot disable. Where should the instruction live?
options: In each repository's ./CLAUDE.md, copied into every project.
In each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md user memory.
In the enterprise managed CLAUDE.md file (for example /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md), which takes precedence over lower layers.
In ./CLAUDE.local.md inside every working copy.
questions.why: — The managed enterprise file is deployed centrally and takes precedence over every lower layer. A per-repo copy is editable and unenforced; user memory is per-developer and removable; and CLAUDE.local.md is gitignored and reaches no one else.

questions.stem: A CI job must run Claude Code unattended, have its output parsed by a script, and make no interactive prompts. Which invocation is most effective?
options: Run claude interactively and pipe keystrokes to it.
Run claude --resume and wait for a human to approve edits.
Add the instructions to CLAUDE.md and run claude with no flags.
Run claude -p "..." with a structured output format such as JSON (headless mode).
questions.why: — Headless -p with a structured output format is purpose-built for unattended, parseable runs. Interactive piping needs a terminal; --resume restores a session for a person to drive; and CLAUDE.md shapes behavior but does not make a run non-interactive.

questions.stem: A service calling the Messages API is seeing a mix of errors under load: 429 rate_limit_error, occasional 529 overloaded responses, and — after a bad deploy — a 400 invalid_request_error and a 401 authentication_error. Which handling is most effective?
options: Retry only the 429 and 529 (transient) with backoff, and fail fast on the 400 and 401 so the malformed request and bad credentials surface immediately.
Retry all four error types with backoff so the service recovers automatically without operator intervention.
Increase max_tokens and retry every failed request, since a larger response budget may avoid the errors.
Disable retries entirely and surface every error to the caller, so the service never amplifies load on the API.
questions.why: — Only the transient failures can succeed on a later attempt, so they get backoff retries while the deterministic client errors fail fast and stay visible. Retrying all four loops forever on the 400 and 401; raising max_tokens touches none of the causes; and disabling retries turns a spike into downtime.

questions.stem: An engineer sends a long contract in one Claude API call and asks for a summary. The request fails with a context-length error, and an earlier shorter attempt returned a summary that silently omitted the last third of the document. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Switch to the largest model available, since a bigger model must accept the whole contract.
Increase max_tokens until the whole contract fits and the error goes away.
Measure the input in tokens, keep system prompt, history, tools, and document inside the context window, and chunk or summarize the document so nothing is dropped.
Paste the document twice so the model is more likely to read all of it.
questions.why: — The context window is a hard token budget shared by every part of the request, so the fix is to count tokens and fit or chunk the input. A larger model is not a guaranteed fix for an oversized input; max_tokens caps output, not input; and repeating the document doubles the overflow.

questions.stem: A team's support classifier passes on every prompt they try by hand, but occasionally misfiles tickets in production, and a scheduled model upgrade is weeks away. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Set temperature to 0 and ship, because deterministic sampling removes the variation.
Pin the current model version, build a labelled eval set, measure accuracy on it, and re-run the eval against any new model version before promoting it.
Add an instruction telling the model to always classify correctly and never make mistakes.
Upgrade to the newest model immediately so the upgrade happens before the deadline.
questions.why: — Nondeterminism means accuracy is established by measuring on a representative set, and pinning plus re-evaluating turns a model change into a controlled release. Temperature 0 reduces but does not remove variance; an instruction to 'always be correct' adds no information; and upgrading first is the unmeasured change the eval exists to catch.

questions.stem: A chat UI built with an Anthropic SDK helper waits for the full response before rendering and appears to hang until the answer is complete. Time-to-first-token is the metric the team cares about. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Increase the request timeout so the UI eventually gets the full body and renders it.
Switch to a smaller model so the whole answer arrives faster in one piece.
Consume the streamed server-sent events as they arrive and render each increment, rather than waiting for a single complete JSON response.
Disable streaming and poll the API repeatedly until the answer is ready.
questions.why: — Streaming returns incremental events, so handling each one renders the first tokens immediately. A longer timeout just makes the user wait; a smaller model still returns one body; and disabling streaming and polling adds latency and cost.

questions.stem: A product sends three workloads to the most capable model: (1) tagging each of 200,000 messages per day with one of eight intent labels, (2) reviewing pull requests, and (3) analysing complex legal clauses where errors are costly. Cost and latency matter for workload 1. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Keep all three on the top model, since a single consistent model is simpler to operate.
Move all three to the cheapest tier and accept some accuracy loss on legal analysis to minimise cost.
Move all three to the cheapest tier but disable extended thinking everywhere to save tokens.
Route the high-volume, well-specified tagging to the fast cheap tier, keep a mid-tier model for code review, and reserve the top tier for the complex legal analysis.
questions.why: — Tier by task: simple high-volume tagging fits the fast cheap tier, code review a balanced mid-tier, and costly nuanced legal work the top tier. A single top model pays for unused capability; cheapest-everywhere and disabling thinking degrade the workload that needs quality.

questions.stem: A coding assistant sends an identical 20,000-token system prompt and tool-definition block on every one of thousands of daily requests, with only the user's question changing. The team wants to lower cost without reducing answer quality. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Cache the user's question on each call, since that is the part that differs.
Shorten the system prompt and tool definitions by deleting rules until the token count drops.
Disable caching and reduce max_tokens so every response is shorter.
Mark the stable system-and-tools block as cacheable so repeated calls read it at a fraction of the input rate, and keep the changing user question outside the cached prefix.
questions.why: — The cost is a large unchanging prefix, which is exactly what prompt caching is for. Caching the volatile question writes a cache it never reuses; deleting rules trades quality for tokens; and disabling caching leaves the big prefix at full price.

questions.stem: A team cannot explain why their Claude bill is high and is guessing token counts from character length. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Estimate tokens as characters divided by four and multiply by the price.
Switch to the cheapest model and assume cost scales down proportionally.
Read the usage fields in the response (input tokens, output tokens, cache read/write) as the source of truth and budget from those.
Disable prompt caching to avoid the write premium.
questions.why: — The response usage fields are the source of truth for input, output, and cache tokens, so cost should be measured from them. Estimating from character count is guesswork; assuming cost scales with model tier is unmeasured; and disabling caching removes a saving rather than explaining the bill.

questions.stem: An application needs a persistent, push-style interactive connection rather than request/response calls. Which transport choice is most appropriate?
options: Poll the REST endpoint every second to simulate a push channel.
Use a persistent transport such as websockets for interactive, push-style integration, and keep request/response REST for batch and tool-calling work.
Use the Message Batches API for the interactive connection.
Increase the REST timeout so the connection stays open.
questions.why: — Persistent, push-style interactivity is what websockets are for, while REST fits request/response batch and tool-calling work. Polling simulates push at needless cost; the Batch API is for latency-tolerant bulk; and a longer timeout does not create a push channel.

questions.stem: A simple classification task is paying for extended thinking and is slow; the labels are simple and the volume is high. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Keep extended thinking but lower the temperature.
Move the task to the top model with extended thinking enabled.
Add more few-shot examples and keep extended thinking.
Use a fast, low-effort mode (no extended thinking) for the simple high-volume classification.
questions.why: — A simple, high-volume classification should run in a fast, low-effort mode without extended thinking. Keeping thinking and lowering temperature still pays the latency; moving to the top tier overspends; and more examples do not justify thinking on an easy task.

questions.stem: Costs are driven by long, rambling answers even though inputs are short. Which change most directly reduces cost?
options: Increase max_tokens so answers finish in one pass.
Set a deliberate max_tokens and constrain output length, since output tokens are typically the pricier side of the bill.
Enable caching on the output tokens to reduce their cost.
Switch models without measuring, since a different model must be cheaper.
questions.why: — Output tokens are typically the pricier side of the bill, so a deliberate max_tokens and constrained output is the cost lever. Raising max_tokens invites longer answers; output cannot be cached the way a stable prefix can; and switching models without measuring is guesswork.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into a codebase investigation the agent starts describing 'typical patterns' instead of the classes and files it found earlier, gives inconsistent answers about the same module, and begins assuming instead of checking. The exploration will continue for another hour across unfamiliar code. Which approach is most effective?
options: Switch to a model with a larger context window so the earlier findings stay resident.
Restart the investigation from a clean context and re-run the earlier exploration with tighter prompts.
Have the agent write key findings — file:line, entry points, known issues — to a scratchpad file and consult it for later questions.
Raise the model temperature so responses stay specific rather than generic.
questions.why: — A scratchpad externalises the findings so they survive compaction and are re-readable when the agent drifts. A larger window treats dilution as capacity; restarting re-runs the same work into the same wall; and temperature changes sampling, not retention.

questions.stem: An agentic coding loop has run sixty turns, each appending a full forty-field API response. The model now ignores the constraints set at the start even though those constraints are still in the transcript. The work must continue with the same constraints, and the state cannot be cheaply re-derived. Which approach is most effective?
options: Prune each tool result to the fields the next decision needs, compact the history into a structured summary of decisions and constraints, and continue from it.
Increase the context window so the full transcript and every tool result stay resident.
Restart from a clean context and re-derive the state by re-running the earlier turns.
Raise the summarization threshold so compaction triggers later in the run.
questions.why: — The failure is noise plus a lossy continuation, so the fix is to stop noise entering (prune) and carry decisions forward (compact). A larger window keeps the noise resident; re-deriving repeats work already in the transcript; and raising the threshold only delays compaction.

questions.stem: A code-review prompt instructs the model to 'be conservative when flagging issues' and to 'only report high-confidence findings.' Reviewers report inconsistent results and a high false-positive rate, and they have started ignoring all warnings. Which approach is most effective?
options: Replace the vague criterion with explicit criteria that define what qualifies as reportable and what does not, including the boundary cases that must not be flagged.
Raise the model temperature so it makes more nuanced judgment calls.
Add a confidence-score threshold and route anything below it to a human reviewer.
Add several more examples of past reviews without changing the criterion.
questions.why: — The root cause is an underspecified criterion, so the durable fix defines qualifying and disqualifying conditions. Temperature changes sampling and reduces consistency; a confidence threshold filters after the fact; and more examples of past reviews still rest on the same ambiguity.

questions.stem: An extraction prompt describes the output schema in careful prose, but the model keeps placing edge cases in the wrong category and inventing values for fields that are absent from the source document. Which approach is most effective?
options: Rewrite the instruction in more detail, restating the schema a second time.
Add two to four worked examples — input, correct output, and the reasoning — including one where the correct output is null because the value is absent.
Lower the temperature to zero so the output becomes deterministic.
Add a confidence field and discard any extraction that falls below a threshold.
questions.why: — The failures are about shape and boundary, which worked examples with reasoning teach directly, including a null case for absent data. More description restates a clear rule; lower temperature repeats the same wrong shape; and a confidence field does not tell the model the correct output.

questions.stem: An invoice extraction service uses a strict schema and returns schema-valid JSON on every request, but the stated total sometimes does not equal the sum of the line items, and downstream reconciliation fails. Which approach is most effective?
options: Enable strict mode on the schema so the model cannot return an inconsistent total.
Increase max_tokens so the model has more room to compute the total correctly.
Add semantic validation after extraction: recompute the total from the line items and, on a mismatch, retry with the specific discrepancy fed back to the model.
Parse the model's free-text reasoning and use whichever total it describes.
questions.why: — Strict mode guarantees schema compliance, not that the arithmetic is right, so the fix is semantic validation with a retry that names the specific error. Strict mode is already on and cannot enforce cross-field arithmetic; more output tokens does not recompute the sum; and parsing free-text reasoning abandons the constrained channel.

questions.stem: A developer is tuning a prompt and is unsure where each part should live so it stays authoritative across calls. Which placement is most effective?
options: Put everything in the user turn so it sits closest to the data.
Put the task data in the system prompt and the rules in the user turn.
Repeat the rules in every user turn and remove them from the system prompt.
Put the durable role and rules in the system prompt and the task data and one-off constraints in the user turn.
questions.why: — Durable role and rules belong in the system prompt, while task data and one-off constraints belong in the user turn. Putting rules in the user turn weakens their authority; swapping the two misplaces both; and repeating rules in every turn without a system prompt removes the stable, authoritative placement.

questions.stem: A Claude-powered agent summarizes web pages submitted by end users. One page contains hidden text instructing the model to ignore previous instructions, reveal its system prompt, and call a tool that posts to the user's account. Which mitigation is most effective?
options: Raise the model's temperature so its behavior becomes harder to predict and to steer.
Add a line to the system prompt asking users not to include malicious instructions in their submissions.
Treat retrieved page content as untrusted input, keep it separate from trusted instructions, and use guardrails or hooks so injected text cannot trigger sensitive actions.
Switch to a larger, more capable model that follows instructions more reliably.
questions.why: — The root cause is that untrusted content reached the instruction channel and could drive a side-effecting tool, so separating data from instructions and gating the tool fixes it at the boundary. Raising temperature adds no control; a prompt line lives in the same channel the attacker wrote into; and a larger model still obeys the same injection.

questions.stem: A team ships a customer-support agent and wants full observability. An engineer proposes logging every system prompt, user message, model completion, and tool payload in plaintext to a shared log service. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Log the full prompt and completion for every request so that any incident can be reconstructed exactly.

Log operational metadata such as request IDs, token counts, error categories, and timings, and redact or tokenize PII and secrets before anything is persisted, with access controls and a retention limit.
Log only the model's completions, since prompts are less sensitive than outputs.
Disable logging entirely so that no sensitive data is ever written anywhere.
questions.why: — Persisting prompts and completions in plaintext turns a transient exposure into a durable, widely-readable breach, so the right move is least-privilege logging with redaction. Full logging is the liability itself; logging only completions still retains PII; and disabling logging removes observability without addressing redaction.

questions.stem: A public assistant must block disallowed content and must never let a conversation trigger a refund or an outbound email. The only current control is a system-prompt sentence that says never to do those things, and users still occasionally get through. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Deploy guardrails at three layers: classify input against policy, gate side-effecting tool calls with allowlists and approval, and validate output before it is shown or sent.
Rewrite the system prompt in stronger, more explicit language and add examples of forbidden requests.
Raise the model's refusal threshold by switching to a more safety-tuned model.
Log every disallowed request and review the logs weekly to remove the abuse after the fact.
questions.why: — The boundary fails because a single probabilistic layer does all the work, so the fix distributes control across input, tool-call, and output. Stronger prompt wording is the same leaked mechanism; a more safety-tuned model is still one layer that does not gate the tool; and log-and-review is detective, not preventive.

questions.stem: A developer needs an internal tool to call a vendor API and proposes hard-coding the vendor key in the source file, pasting it into the system prompt, and 'cleaning it up later.' Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Hard-code the key in the source for now and move it to a secret manager before the production release.
Put the key in the system prompt so the model can pass it directly to the API on each call.

Store the key in a secret manager, inject it via an environment variable at runtime, scope it least-privilege, and rotate it; the model calls a server-side tool that uses the key so it never enters the prompt.
Commit the key to a private repository, since the repository is not public.
questions.why: — Keeping the key in a secret manager, injected at runtime and scoped least-privilege, is the only option that keeps it out of code, prompts, and logs while bounding the blast radius. Hard-coding 'for now' leaves the key in git history; a prompt is an echoed channel; and a private repo is still committed source.

questions.stem: An agent has two tools: get_customer described as 'Gets customer information' and get_customer_orders described as 'Gets customer data'. Asked to list a customer's recent orders, Claude frequently calls get_customer and then reports it cannot find the orders. Which approach is most effective?
options: Rewrite both descriptions to state precisely what each returns and when to use it, so get_customer covers profile details and get_customer_orders covers order history, with no overlap.
Merge the two tools into one get_customer that returns profile and orders together, and let the model pick out the fields it needs.
Add a third tool that lists customers together with their orders, so an always-applicable option exists.
Raise max_tokens so the model has more room to reason about which tool to pick.
questions.why: — The confusion is a description problem: both tools describe themselves almost identically, so distinct descriptions fix selection. Merging forces the model to infer fields; a third lookalike tool adds ambiguity; and raising max_tokens changes nothing because the model is not out of room, it is out of signal.

questions.stem: An agent calls an update_invoice tool. When a caller sends an amount as the string '1,200.00', the handler throws a database error, the tool returns the raw exception text, and the agent calls the same tool with the same string again, looping. Which approach is most effective?
options: Validate the argument against the schema and, on failure, return a structured error stating that amount must be a number without separators, flagged with is_error, so the model can correct the call.
Have the tool coerce any value it receives into the correct type and proceed, so the call never fails.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to always pass valid arguments.
Increase the retry limit so the agent has more attempts to get the argument right.
questions.why: — Structured validation catches the bad value at the boundary and the specific message tells the model how to fix it, so the retry succeeds. Silent coercion can write a wrong amount; a prompt instruction does not explain the failure; and a higher retry limit repeats the same opaque error.

questions.stem: A team needs Claude to call an internal inventory service exposed as a REST API. The capability must be reusable across several Claude applications and maintained independently of any one app. Which approach is most effective?
options: Hard-code the inventory logic into each application's system prompt.
Paste the current inventory data into the context window on every request.
Rely on a built-in tool, since built-in tools can reach any internal REST API.
Build an MCP server that exposes the inventory operations as tools, so multiple applications can connect to the same server.
questions.why: — The stem names reuse across applications and independent maintenance, which is exactly what an MCP server provides. Hard-coding is neither reusable nor maintainable; pasting data gives no live access; and built-in tools do not reach arbitrary internal APIs.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to follow a fixed review checklist every time it reviews a pull request. The checklist is pure procedure: no external system is contacted and no live data is needed. A developer proposes building an MCP server to expose the checklist. Which approach is most effective?
options: Build the MCP server, since exposing the checklist as a tool guarantees Claude follows it.
Express the checklist as a Skill or project instructions that shape how the model reviews, since no executable capability or external access is required.
Write a custom tool that returns the checklist text when the model calls it.
Add the checklist as a new built-in tool.
questions.why: — A checklist is behavior, not capability, so a Skill or project instructions carries it with no maintenance. An MCP server and a custom tool both add runtime for something that is only text; and a built-in tool is not something a developer can add.

questions.stem: A support agent is given access to every tool in the company, including order lookup, billing, inventory, deployment and HR, so it can handle anything. Tool selection is now unreliable and each request is expensive. Which approach is most effective?
options: Scope the agent to the small set of tools its job needs, with distinct descriptions, and let other agents own the other capabilities.
Add more tools to cover the cases the agent currently gets wrong.
Keep all sixty tools but raise max_tokens so the model can reason over the full list.
Merge all sixty tools into one tool that takes a mode parameter.
questions.why: — Selection degrades as the tool set grows and overlaps, and every schema costs context on every request, so scoping fixes both accuracy and cost. Adding more tools increases ambiguity; a larger max_tokens pays more for the same over-broad set; and one mode-parameter tool hides distinct capabilities behind a vague description.

questions.stem: A team wants an MCP client application to attach a set of internal documents to the model's context, addressed by URI, without the model calling a function for each one. Which approach is most effective?
options: Expose each document as a separate model-invoked tool.
Expose the documents as MCP resources (application-controlled context addressed by URI) rather than as tools.
Expose the documents as MCP prompts the user selects.
Paste the document contents into the system prompt at build time.
questions.why: — Resources are application-controlled context addressed by URI, so the client can attach documents without the model calling a function. Exposing each document as a tool makes the model invoke it; prompts are user-invoked templates; and pasting at build time gives no live, addressable resource.
